articles.title: We made a multiplayer browser game with no game server
articles.excerpt: Super Nova Arena is a small PvP game that runs in a browser tab. Your mouse is your player, a glowing star. Pull back, let go, and you sling a shot at someone else. Space puts up a shield, right click…
articles.body: Super Nova Arena is a small PvP game that runs in a browser tab. Your mouse is your player, a glowing star. Pull back, let go, and you sling a shot at someone else. Space puts up a shield, right click (or Q) drops a mine, and after 90 seconds whoever has the most KOs wins. Up to 8 people can share a lobby. The part I actually want to talk about is the plumbing, because there isn't any. No game server, no backend at all. The site is a static page on GitHub Pages and players connect straight to each other. How the connecting works We use Trystero with its Nostr strategy. Public Nostr relays only help peers find each other, and once they have, everything goes over WebRTC directly between players.

articles.body: What I taught at Google DevFest 2026, written up as a practical playbook: decide the goal, curate the evidence, and use Gemini, Google AI Studio, Antigravity, and Cloud Run to make it live. Most portfolios fail for a simple reason. They show work, but they don't make a decision easier for the person looking at them. A recruiter has about a minute. A potential client wants to know whether you can solve their problem. Neither wants a gallery of everything you have ever made. They want answers to three questions: who is this person, is their work relevant to me, and what do I do next? At DevFest 2026, I gave a session built around that idea. The first half is design strategy. The second half is engineering: turning that strategy into a deployed website with AI-assisted development.

articles.title: How to Convert an Image to DXF for CNC Cutting (and When Auto-Trace Falls Short)
articles.excerpt: Your cutting machine doesn't care about pixels. A JPG or PNG is a grid of colored dots. It looks like a logo or a part, but there is nothing in it a laser, plasma torch or router bit can follow. What…
articles.body: Your cutting machine doesn't care about pixels. A JPG or PNG is a grid of colored dots. It looks like a logo or a part, but there is nothing in it a laser, plasma torch or router bit can follow. What the machine needs is a vector file: lines and curves with exact coordinates, which is what a DXF holds. So "converting an image to DXF" really means tracing the picture into paths. You can do that yourself with free or common software, and for simple, bold shapes it works well. For other jobs, the trace is only the start. Here's how to do it, what to check afterward, and how to tell when a redraw is the better route. What makes a DXF cut-ready Before you trace anything, know what you're aiming for. A DXF that cuts cleanly has: Closed outlines.

articles.title: How moon dust and recycled cardboard could help NASA build its lunar base
articles.excerpt: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface.
articles.body: The high cost of building on the moon has led to wide-ranging research on how to make use of the moon's most plentiful resource: the dusty regolith that covers its surface. Right now, lunar shipping runs about $544,000 per pound ($1.2 million per kilogram), so anything that astronauts can make on the moon using existing materials could help a lot. Scientists have already proposed using regolith for building 3D-printed bricks , solar arrays , and even as soil to grow potatoes . Now, a team of researchers from Purdue University in Indiana have developed an aerogel made from simulated regolith for insulating lunar habitats. New aerogels created by Purdue University researchers, made of cellulose and lunar regolith simulant, could pave the way for insulating materials made on the moon.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 28, 1967: Astronomers Jocelyn Bell and Antony Hewish disover the 1st pulsar with Little Green Men 1 signal
articles.excerpt: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar and they called the signal Little Green Men 1. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On November 28, 1967, astronomers found the first pulsar. A pulsar is a super-dense star that rotates super fast. As the pulsar spins, it emits two beams of light in opposite directions. When astronomers look at a pulsar, it looks like a star that's flickering on and off at a steady, constant pace. The first pulsar was observed by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish. They were looking at the constellation Vulpecula when they saw a star flickering with regular pulses separated by 1.33 seconds. At first they had no idea what it was, so they jokingly nicknamed the signal Little Green Men 1. After more pulsars were discovered, they were able to rule out aliens. This chart tracked the signal of the first pulsar ever discoverered on Nov. 28, 1967.

articles.title: 12 grains of dust found high in Earth's atmosphere reveal secrets of water at the edge of the solar system
articles.excerpt: Grains of dust found floating in Earth's stratosphere hold the secrets of a special kind of 'heavy' water that seems to be abundant in the outer solar system.
articles.body: A dozen grains of dust that have wandered in from the distant Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune were found floating in Earth's stratosphere. And it turns out they hold the secrets of a special kind of 'heavy' water that seems to be surprisingly abundant in the outer solar system. When analyzed by a team of scientists the 12 dust grains, which were captured by NASA's stratospheric ER-2 research aircraft, show signs of having interacted with a form of water that contains heavy oxygen isotopes. This is important because to better understand how the planets formed, scientists are seeking to understand how various materials were distributed around the early solar system 4.5 billion years ago.
